elements.element: New York law governs the Agreement.
elements.evidence: Section 18.3 is retained unchanged: "shall be governed by, and construed and enforced in accordance with, the laws of the State of New York, United States, without reference to conflict of law principles." The redline does not touch the choice-of-law words, which is exactly what the redline guidance requires.

elements.element: State and federal courts in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction over the merits, subject only to temporary injunctive relief elsewhere.
elements.evidence: New Section 17.3(a): "The state and federal courts located in New York County, New York shall have exclusive jurisdiction over the merits of any Dispute, provided that either Party may apply to any other court of competent jurisdiction for temporary injunctive relief. Sections 17.3(b) through (g) shall not apply." The alternate-forum carve-out is limited to temporary injunctive relief (the permitted customary carve-out), the ICC/Osaka seat provision is gone, and the residual arbitral subsections are expressly disapplied so no competing mandatory arbitral forum survives. The pre-existing chapeau carve-outs (Expert determinations under 17.2 and inventorship disputes) are untouched pre-redline scope limits on the referral, not new alternate merits forums created by this edit; they are noted rather than treated as a failure.

elements.element: The governing law is Delaware, California, or England and Wales.
elements.evidence: Section 18.3 selects the laws of the State of New York. No Delaware, California, or England and Wales law is designated. This is expected and harmless because the proposal targets the preferred level, which sits above the fallback.

elements.element: The dispute forum is the corresponding Delaware or California courts, or the courts of London for England and Wales law.
elements.evidence: The new forum is the state and federal courts in New York County; no Delaware, California, or London courts are named. Again this is a consequence of proposing the preferred position rather than the fallback.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: New York law was already in place and untouched, and the new Section 17.3(a) supplies exclusive New York County state and federal court jurisdiction over the merits with only a temporary-injunctive-relief carve-out to other courts.

The classification as a deviation is correct on the forum limb: original Section 17.3(a) imposed mandatory, exclusive three-arbitrator ICC arbitration seated in Osaka whenever Array demanded it, i.e. mandatory arbitration capable of a seat outside the accepted list, which is walk-away territory and not curable at the fallback.

Minimality holds. The edit replaces only the referral language and the ICC/seat subsection, converts the heading to match, and adds the single disapplication sentence needed to switch off the residual arbitral machinery. Section 18.3, the Expert and inventorship carve-outs, and the CISG exclusion are all retained verbatim; no extra procedures, damages categories, or boilerplate were added.

Intent is preserved on the operative level: nothing live now contradicts the New York court forum, the party-level right to seek interim relief from a court is carried forward into 17.3(a), and no cross-reference is left dangling (17.3(g)'s reference to Section 18.3 still resolves).

Cleanup point the drafter should make before sending: retained Section 17.3(g) still speaks of the "Arbitration Tribunal", "the Agreement to arbitrate" and "the right to arbitrate", but the sentence that defined "Arbitration Tribunal" and "Rules" sat in the deleted 17.3(a). Although 17.3(a) expressly disapplies (b) through (g) so the text is inert, the defined term is now orphaned. Strike Sections 17.3(b) through (g) outright (or delete (g) and keep only the disapplication for (b)-(f)) rather than leaving dead arbitral text with an undefined term.

Secondary check: confirm no other section of the Agreement cross-refers to "arbitration", the "Arbitration Tribunal", or Section 17.3(b)-(g) (for example escalation in 17.1/17.2, confidentiality, or enforcement provisions). Any such surviving reference would need conforming amendment to avoid a dangling cross-reference.

Residual note, not a deviation: the chapeau still lets either Party "pursue such remedies as it may deem necessary or appropriate" for inventorship disputes, so those disputes fall outside the exclusive New York forum. That carve-out pre-dates the redline and removing it would breach minimality, so flag it in the rationale only.
Comment tone and content are compliant: concise, first person plural, states what changed and why, and cites the accepted-jurisdiction-courts position without lecturing.
